title: Rio Grande County well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: In Rio Grande County the median well depth is 100 ft with a 15 gpm median yield. Learn what that means for new well drilling costs and water supply.
h1: Water wells in Rio Grande County, Colorado
intro_html:
Rio Grande County wells are generally on the shallow side for Colorado, but there’s a wide spread once you get away from the main San Luis Valley floor. Looking at thousands of permits here gives a pretty clear picture of how deep you’re likely to drill, how much water most wells make, and what that usually costs.

If you’re buying land or planning a new home around Monte Vista, Del Norte, South Fork, or the outlying ranch areas, the numbers below are what I’d use to plan a well and budget.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in Rio Grande County
sections.html:
The typical well in Rio Grande County is not extremely deep by Colorado standards. The median total depth is 100 feet, and half of all wells fall between 60 and 180 feet. About 48% of wells are under 100 feet, another 40% are 100–300 feet, 10% run 300–600 feet, and roughly 3% go past 600 feet. The deepest on record goes down 3,022 feet, which tells you how much things can vary once you’re off the main aquifer.

For a new domestic well, I’d usually budget in that 60–180 foot band unless nearby wells show something different. In rougher fractured-bedrock areas, you plan for the possibility of going a couple hundred feet deeper if you have to chase water.

sections.heading: Well yield and how much water you can expect
sections.html:
Production here is generally strong. The median reported pump yield is 15 gpm, with the middle half of wells between 12 and 50 gpm. Only about 1% of wells report under 1 gpm, and 3% report 1–5 gpm. On the higher side, 28% are 5–15 gpm and a big share, 69%, are at 15 gpm or more.

For a single-family exempt household well, anything around 5 gpm and up is workable if the well is built right. With Rio Grande County’s yield numbers, most domestic and stock wells have plenty of capacity; the lower-yield outliers are what you watch for when you review neighboring permits.

sections.heading: Water table depth and long-term trend
sections.html:
Static water levels are generally shallow. The median depth to water is 29 feet, with the middle half of wells between 12 and 69 feet below ground. That means a lot of pumps don’t have to work very hard, which helps with long-term operating costs.

Over time, median static levels have moved from 12 feet in the 1960s to 15 in the 1970s, 20 in the 1980s, then around 31 feet in the 2000s. The 2010s came in at 28 feet, and the 2020s are about 30 feet. That points to a water table that’s deeper than it used to be, but not in a sharp, rapid drop. Still, I’d always look at the most recent nearby measurements before committing to a shallow pump design.

sections.heading: Who is drilling here and when wells went in
sections.html:
Rio Grande County has a long drilling history, with 9,740 well permits on record and 6,998 listed as constructed. Drilling really picked up in the 1970s and 1990s, with 1,348 permits in the 1970s and 1,518 in the 1990s. The 2000s were the busiest so far at 1,670 permits, then about 725 in the 2010s and 697 already in the 2020s, with permits issued through 2026.

Most wells are in unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers (7,429 wells) and the Unconfined San Luis Valley aquifer system (over 1,400 wells across the two naming variants). The main drillers on record are Valley Pump Company (Self, Clinton L.), Irrigation Engineering & Supp. (Burk, Coy), and L D Spencer Drilling And Pump. Checking what those drillers hit on nearby permits is one of the best ways to set expectations for a specific parcel.

sections.heading: What a new well typically costs in Rio Grande County
sections.html:
Ground conditions here are mostly mixed sedimentary and alluvial, so drilling is fairly predictable. The going rate in the cost model is about $50–$75 per foot. At the county’s 100-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole alone around $5,000–$7,500.

By the time you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a finished domestic well at that median depth usually falls in the $11,000–$19,500 range. If nearby wells run closer to 180–300 feet instead of 100, scale those numbers up accordingly when you budget or negotiate a land price.

sections.heading: Risks and checks: quality, yield, and building layout
sections.html:
On the production side, only 1% of wells report under 1 gpm and 3% fall in the 1–5 gpm range, but those low-yield wells are still important to watch for in your immediate area. Most permits list use as domestic/household (59%), stock (19%), irrigation (26%), and monitoring (4%), so you’ll often see a mix of heavier irrigation wells and smaller domestic wells around you.

There are mapped environmental concerns: 19 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 8 historic mine features, and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. That doesn’t mean your water is bad, but it does mean you should plan on a full lab test panel on any existing well and design your septic and building locations with good separation from the well.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a lot in Rio Grande County
sections.html:
If you’re looking at land around Monte Vista, Del Norte, South Fork, Alpine, or the open country between, start by pulling nearby well permits from the state database. Compare depths to the county’s 60–180 foot middle range and check the reported gpm against the 12–50 gpm middle band.

Confirm whether the parcel is eligible for an exempt household well and what other uses (stock or limited irrigation) are allowed under that permit. In the San Luis Valley over-appropriated areas, larger irrigation or commercial uses can require augmentation. Before closing, I’d want: a drilling or pump contractor’s opinion based on local logs, a realistic cost range using the $50–$75 per foot model, and written contingency language if a new well comes in shallow, low-yield, or needs to be redrilled.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Rio Grande County, Colorado?
faq.a: Across Rio Grande County, the median well depth is about 100 feet, with half of wells between 60 and 180 feet. Around 48% of wells are under 100 feet, and another 40% are 100–300 feet. Only about 13% go deeper than 300 feet, and roughly 3% exceed 600 feet. For most home sites, planning in that 60–180 foot range is a reasonable starting point, then adjust based on nearby well records.

faq.q: What is a typical well yield in Rio Grande County?
faq.a: Reported yields here are generally strong. The median pump yield is 15 gpm, with the middle half of wells between 12 and 50 gpm. Only about 1% of wells report less than 1 gpm and 3% are in the 1–5 gpm range. About 28% produce 5–15 gpm and roughly 69% are 15 gpm or higher. For a single-family household well, those numbers usually provide plenty of water when the system is designed correctly.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Rio Grande County?
faq.a: In Rio Grande County’s mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground, the cost model shows about $50–$75 per foot to drill. At the county’s 100-foot median depth, that puts the bare hole around $5,000–$7,500. A complete domestic well with casing, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical typically runs in the $11,000–$19,500 range at that depth. Deeper wells, say up toward 180–300 feet, will scale those costs up proportionally.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Rio Grande County?
faq.a: Safety depends on the specific well. There are 19 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 8 historic mine features, and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup locations within about 10 miles, so some areas warrant closer attention. The state does not test private wells automatically. For any existing or new well, plan on a full water quality lab test and consider periodic retesting, especially if you’re near mapped industrial, mining, or agricultural activity.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping in Rio Grande County wells?
faq.a: Median static water levels have deepened compared to the 1960s, when the median depth to water was about 12 feet. That moved to 15 feet in the 1970s, 20 feet in the 1980s, and around 31 feet in the 2000s. In the 2010s the median was about 28 feet, and in the 2020s it’s around 30 feet. So the overall trend is to a deeper water table than decades ago, but not a sharp, continuous decline in the recent data.
